synopsis: Scalar-output agreement compares a simulation result with its physical-test counterpart using absolute difference divided by the measured value, usually against a pre-agreed percentage band; an illustrative stopping-distance comparison of 38.0 m measured versus 39.5 m simulated gives 3.9% error [f14727, f14728, f14731]. For heavy off-road automatic braking, the booklet recommends stopping-distance, intervention-time, residual impact-speed, range and relative-speed errors, but requires scalar checks to be combined with timing, waveform, distribution and outcome evidence [f14737, f8042]. Scalar agreement alone can be misleading: one aviation comparison had only 0.3% peak error but 60.4% time-history error, and equal peak decelerations can still produce different collision outcomes if their timing differs [f7555, f14736]. Aviation guidance uses application-specific 10% criteria, and one example achieved 3.42% peak error and 7.2% time-history error; the booklet explicitly warns against adopting 10% as a generic off-road braking tolerance [f7777, f7782, f7779]. Acceptance bands must also account for uncertainty: in the aircraft-seat example, a 1,500 lb limit and approximately 42 lb standard deviation require a prediction below about 1,431 lb for 95% confidence, so a nominal prediction of 1,490 lb is insufficient [f14732, f14733, f14734, f14735].
